The “Afro” part isn’t claiming most people are born in Africa. It’s pointing to the African roots of a lot of black Americans, especially the trans-Atlantic slave trade and the communities that grew up in the US. You’re mixing up ancestry and birthplace. That distinction matters.

The label “Afro-American” or “African American” became common in the 1960s and after, as people wanted a term that recognized African roots without making everyone sound like they were just visitors from the continent. So it’s more about heritage than where someone actually came from.

The thing people usually get wrong is treating it as a claim that every black American is literally from Africa. It’s not. Most are American, full stop. The “Afro” part is an acknowledgement of the ancestral connection, which can be hard to trace through slavery and mixed histories.

If you want a quick practical way to think about it: ancestry isn’t birthplace, and that’s the whole point of the name.

Spending hours in crowded malls and listening to your wife ask for opinions on thirty different pairs of shoes really taxes your neck and jaw. Your brain ends up turning that continuous stress into a weird dull ache. It's just your body's way of saying it is completely exhausted and overstimulated.

Hey Sam,

Good questions. House buying is more paperwork than you expect. The first thing to sort is financing. If you're borrowing, get a pre-approval before you start looking, because sellers are more likely to take you seriously with one. Don't just assume you qualify for what you want, since the lender sets the ceiling.

The thing people usually mess up is thinking the sale price is the real cost. Factor in stamp duty, conveyance fees, inspections, moving costs, and possibly a small emergency fund. I think it's easy to get excited about a pretty kitchen and forget the boring stuff.

On inspections, don't skip them. A structural or water issue can cost a lot to fix, and a buyer's report can also give you leverage on price. At least that's how it was explained to me.

One more: don't sign anything until the contract actually matches what was agreed verbally.

Also, location costs are easy to underestimate. A house a few extra minutes from good transport or shops is worth paying for, but don't overpay just because the street name sounds nice. Check the local council site for school catchments or nearby development plans.

Hey there,

Glad you asked this because I think most people assume a 3 in 1 means three products in one bottle, but it's really a compromise formula. The big point is that the surfactants and conditioning agents are chosen to be mild enough for both skin and hair. A normal shampoo wants stronger cleansing on the scalp, a normal conditioner wants more film forming agents, and a normal body wash wants skin friendly cleansing. The 3 in 1 tries to land somewhere in the middle, so it won't be as good at any one job as the dedicated versions. Compared with a 2 in 1 shampoo/conditioner, the 3 in 1 has to add body washing, which usually means the hair cleaning is milder. You might find it leaves less residue on hair but also cleanses less. If your hair gets very greasy, it may need rinsing twice. The weird part is that some bottles say for hair, body, and face, and then you end up with something that's okay everywhere and great nowhere.

I'd use it for convenience or for people with sensitive skin, but I'd keep a proper conditioner on hand. If your hair is dry or damaged, the built in conditioner helps a bit, but for very thick or curly hair you may want a separate treatment. Also, check the label: some are actually just shampoo and conditioner for body, not a true 3 product.

When we say inbreeding lowers IQ, we are talking about a tendency across many children, not a guarantee for any one child. Cognitive ability is influenced by many inherited factors, and related parents carry overlapping sets of those factors. The important point is that some harmful genetic changes are recessive. A person can carry one copy without showing a problem. When two relatives have children, the odds go up that the child receives the same harmful copy from both sides, which can weaken the inherited cognitive factors. That is the science behind the lower average. The effect is statistical, so some inbred children will be right in the normal range.

When a plane is in an emergency, the crew will tell passengers to brace. This is a specific body position meant to keep you safe during a sudden stop, crash, or rough landing. The idea is to prepare your body for impact so that your head, spine, and internal organs are less likely to get hurt.

The position works by bringing your body into a compact shape. You lower your head toward your knees, tighten your core, and hold on to your seatbelt. This stops you from being thrown forward into the seat or other passengers, and it keeps your neck and back from taking a hard jolt. In a crash, the biggest risk is your body moving violently while the plane stops fast. Bracing reduces that movement, so you are less likely to suffer whiplash, back strain, or internal injuries. Keeping your hands on your legs helps keep you stable. It also helps you stay in your seat. It’s a simple move, but it can make a real difference when things go wrong. The more you practice it, the more natural it becomes, and the better protected you will be if an emergency happens.

Most pre-industrial businesses weren't the global giants we see today. They were just local shops, like a bakery or a blacksmith's shop. They were tied to a single street corner and run by one family. If the family moved or passed away, the business usually closed. They just died out. There just wasn't the money or tech to make them famous globally.

The weird part is people often think old guilds or merchant houses survived, but they mostly didn't. The industrial era brought factories and standardization. That is what let companies grow huge. We have massive global brands today because the industrial revolution gave them the scale to last. Keep that in mind when you look at old company histories.

When you finance through the dealer, the rate they quote can look nice, but it's just an opening number, not the whole cost. The bank might start at a slightly higher headline rate, yet what actually ends up in your wallet depends on the total over the loan. Fees, add-ons, insurance, and the length of the term can flip which option is cheaper. A dealer rate of 4% over 72 months can cost more than a bank at 4.5% over 48 months, because the bank term is shorter and has fewer add-ons attached.

The other thing people get wrong is assuming the dealer's lower rate is the whole story. That "lower" rate usually comes with mandatory extras: a service package, an extended warranty, gap insurance, or a dealer-prep fee. You might be paying for a lower rate with a higher monthly fee.

I also think the real cost lives in how the loan is structured, not the headline. If the dealer's low rate is tied to a longer term, your total interest goes up because interest keeps compounding for more months. That's the part most people miss when they only compare the two percentages.

It's also worth remembering that your bank relationship can lower the bank's rate too. If you already have a checking account, a mortgage, or a line of credit, your bank may offer a small discount. That can make a bank loan cheaper than the dealer's advertised low rate.

So the short answer is: compare total cost of ownership, not just the rate. Add up the interest, fees, and add-ons over the whole loan, and in many cases the bank comes out lower even with a slightly higher rate.

The thing that trips people up is that the body isn't wired like a battery. It's ions doing the work. Cells pump sodium and potassium across their membranes, which creates a charge difference that gets maintained by the sodium-potassium pump. When a nerve cell gets triggered, sodium channels open and a small electrical pulse travels down the fiber. Muscles work the same way, and the heart fires in a sequence that keeps you alive. So the "electricity" in the body is really charged particles moving through membranes, not copper wires. It's tiny, but it's how your body talks to itself.

My take on the whole thing: your head isn't hurting because the bones have pressure. I think the pain comes from the blood vessels around the brain getting stretched, not the skull itself. That's how it was explained to me.

The weird part is that people blame the head like a box that's being squeezed. It's closer to a pulse turning into pain. I keep hearing people say tension hurts like a tight band, but honestly I don't buy that fully.

Dehydration or a bad night's sleep could be playing a role. That's just my guess, could be wrong. Drink some water before you start diagnosing yourself.

We picked this place on Sunday because we had a 10 p.m. show at the same hotel, so it should have been easy. Turned out not. We got there at 7:20 p.m., put our names on their totally useless digital waitlist, and were told to come back to pay at 8:23. We did, but then just stood there until 8:40 p.m. when staff casually said we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15. It was just two of us, and they offered zero solutions. Can't even judge the food since we never actually ate. My point: if the wait runs that far past when you pay, tell people upfront so their night isn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

The buffet didn't have a single person waiting on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., which surprised me. Two people came out to about $130, and that felt pretty steep. Going in, I expected the price to sit around steakhouse money. Afterward, I found out the buffet actually costed more than that estimate.

What threw me was that steak wasn't on the menu at all. At that price I assumed there'd be at least some steak option. The meat side had lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can pick up at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood side had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan legs show up at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't come across rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was jammed up to the next one, so I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and sending pieces flying at the people next door. I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, though I didn't try any.

I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider.

Keeping it is the call I made, and I stand by it. The space bar rattles, and hitting it with the edge of my thumb makes it sound like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so example becomes eexample and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I’m typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don’t ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I’d have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.
